Most coaches have absolutely NO IDEA what they’re actually selling.

They think they’re selling coaching sessions, courses, or some fancy methodology they’ve spent years developing.

But after helping launch over 6,000 high-ticket offers, I’ve learned that people don’t give a damn about any of that.

Think about it.

A business owner working 80 hours a week isn’t looking for another business course.

He wants his TIME back.

A parent worried about their child’s future doesn’t want 12 modules of parenting advice.

They want PEACE OF MIND.

And a coach who’s been stuck at $50K/month for the last two years doesn’t want another mastermind full of random ideas.

They want CLIENTS.

You see what I mean?

People aren’t buying what you do. They’re buying what your work makes possible for them.

And here’s where most coaches screw this up.

They try to sell the same vague promise to everybody because they’re terrified of turning away potential customers.

So instead of saying exactly who they help and what result they deliver, they start talking about “unlocking potential” and “transforming lives.”

What the hell does that even mean?

Look, the more specific you get about WHO you’re helping and WHAT they desperately want, the easier it becomes to sell.

Because when the right person sees your offer, they should immediately think, “Holy shit, that’s exactly what I’ve been looking for.”

That’s what makes a great high-ticket offer.

Not more bonuses, more coaching calls, or another 47 course modules.

A specific outcome that a specific person is willing to pay good money to achieve.

If you’re trying to sell to everyone, don’t be surprised when nobody buys.

You can visualize your dream life every single day and still never build it.

Gratitude can shift your mindset. Visualization can help you focus. But neither one can compensate for a business model that doesn't work.

If you want to build real wealth, you need to answer a much more important question:

What valuable problem can you solve that people are willing to pay you to solve?

Your skills are only the starting point. The real opportunity is turning those skills into an offer that delivers a result your market genuinely wants.

Because if the only thing you're selling is your time, your income will always be limited by how much time you have available.

Build a product or service that delivers meaningful value without requiring you to personally trade every hour for every dollar.

Then you have something that can scale beyond your own time and location.

Manifestation won't build your business for you. A compelling offer gives your ambition something real to work with.

1. Don’t spend 15 minutes talking about yourself. Give them a few quick facts about your experience and explain how you discovered your approach. Your credibility should support the solution, not distract from it.

2. Make your audience feel understood. Before presenting your solution, describe their problems better than they can. Ask specific, emotional questions about what they’re experiencing. When people feel understood, they start trusting you.

3. Reframe the real problem. Show your audience that the problems they’re struggling with are symptoms of something bigger. Introduce the root cause they’ve been overlooking and explain why their previous attempts haven’t worked.

4. Lead with the outcome, not the method. Nobody cares about your course, coaching, or framework yet. They only care about the result. So open your webinar with a clear, desirable outcome and add a curiosity hook that makes people want to keep watching.

5. Shift their beliefs instead of overwhelming them with information. The biggest webinar mistake is teaching everything you know. Your goal is to change how people think about their problem, what’s possible, and what it takes to solve it. That’s what creates buying decisions.

6. Sell the bigger transformation. Don’t just explain how your offer solves their immediate problem. Show them what becomes possible afterward. More freedom, less stress, better relationships, or whatever transformation your audience actually wants.

7. Make booking a call the natural next step. Present two choices: continue struggling with the same problems or explore a different approach. Explain exactly what happens on the call, who it’s for, and who it isn’t for.

1. “You need more followers.” No. You need more paying clients. I’ve seen coaches with massive audiences who can barely pay their bills. Being popular on Instagram and running a profitable business are two completely different things.

2. “You need to lower your prices to get more clients.” No. You need an offer that’s worth paying more for. I’ve helped launch over 6,000 high-ticket offers, and I can tell you that charging less is NOT the solution to a crappy offer.

3. “You need to post content every day.” No. You need a reliable way to turn strangers into clients. You can spend the next three years making Instagram Reels, or you can build a funnel that brings qualified prospects to your calendar.

4. “You need to give away your best information to make sales.” No. Information is practically free now. People aren’t paying you $10,000 to watch videos. They’re paying you to help them get a result they haven’t been able to get on their own.

5. “You need a better sales script.” No. You need to ask better questions. If your prospect doesn’t understand why they need help, no magical closing line is going to save you.

6. “You need to spend more money on ads.” No. If your offer and funnel aren’t converting, increasing your budget just means you’re going to lose money faster.

7. “You need to handle objections better.” No. Most objections should be addressed BEFORE you present your price. The sale is usually won or lost in the first 10 minutes, not the last five.

8. “You need to work harder to scale.” No. If you’re personally handling every sale, every client, and every decision, you’re eventually going to hit a ceiling. Building a bigger business means learning to let other people do things you used to do yourself.

Look, after generating over $100M in high-ticket sales, here’s what I’ve learned.

You don’t have 50 different problems holding your business back.

You have ONE.

You haven’t figured out how to turn clicks into clients at the scale you want.

Fix that first and everything else gets a whole lot easier.

And if you want to learn how to do that follow me.

There’s a reason luxury brands like Cartier don’t just disappear the second you buy

And it’s something I wish more coaches understood

It’s called buyer’s remorse

Look, imagine you just spent $15,000 on a watch

You walk out of the store feeling amazing. You’ve wanted this thing for years, and now it’s finally yours

But the next morning, you wake up and think, “Did I really just spend $15,000 on a WATCH?”

Now you’re questioning the purchase
Maybe you should’ve saved the money
Maybe you didn’t really need it

That’s buyer’s remorse, and the exact same thing happens when somebody enrolls in your $10,000 coaching program

Except here’s where most coaches screw it up

They spend weeks getting someone to buy, but the second the payment goes through, they hand them a login to some course portal and call it a day

And then they’re shocked when that client asks for a refund three days later

Guys, come on

Someone just made a massive investment in themselves, and you’re leaving them alone with their doubts?

Here’s what I’d do instead

1. Make sure they hear from a real human being immediately after enrolling (it has to be an actual person who makes them feel taken care of)

2. Get them moving toward their outcome as quickly as possible (don’t make them spend two weeks watching videos before they actually DO anything)

3. Make the next steps crystal clear ( they should know exactly what happens tomorrow, next week, and what you’re working toward together)

You’re not doing any of this to manipulate somebody into keeping a purchase they regret

You’re doing it because they trusted you to help them solve a serious problem, and your responsibility to that person doesn’t begin at the first coaching call

It begins the moment they enroll

The best way to eliminate buyer’s remorse is to start delivering on the promise you made IMMEDIATELY

And if you do that well, you won’t have to spend nearly as much time convincing clients to stay

She’d been introducing herself the wrong way for 11 years. It took 90 seconds to change everything.

When someone asked what she did, Kate would say, “I’m a personal development coach.”

The problem? That tells people your job title. It doesn’t tell them why they should care.

It doesn’t communicate the problem you solve, the transformation you deliver, or why someone should choose you over the thousands of other coaches out there.

Here’s the shift:

Instead of saying, “I’m a personal development coach,” Kate learned to say:

“I help burnt-out corporate moms thrive at work and show up for their families—without feeling like they have to sacrifice one for the other.”

See the difference?

One describes a profession. The other makes the right person feel understood.

If you’re a coach or expert, stop leading with your title. Start communicating who you help, what problem you solve, and what result you help them achieve.

People don’t buy your job title. They buy the transformation you make possible.

Your last bad hire probably interviewed beautifully. That’s exactly the problem.

Most founders make the same mistake: they hire people they like instead of people who are wired to succeed in the role.

But here’s the catch: the traits that make someone easy to get along with aren’t always the traits that make them great at their job.

Take high-ticket sales.

You might want someone who challenges prospects, pushes back on flawed thinking, and asks uncomfortable questions—not someone whose priority is keeping every conversation pleasant.

That person might even frustrate you during the interview.

And that’s precisely why you need to look beyond chemistry.

Before your next hire, ask yourself:

What behaviors, strengths, and personality traits does this specific role actually require?

Then build your hiring process around those criteria—not around who you’d most enjoy grabbing coffee with.

Stop hiring people you like. Start hiring people who can do the job exceptionally well.

Book the hour. Open the account. Write down what is owed and to whom.

If you sound uncertain when you say your price, your prospect will hear it.

You can have an incredible coaching program, deliver life-changing results, and still undermine the sale in the final few seconds of a sales call.

Why? Because the moment you reveal your price, you start apologizing for it, over explaining it, or rushing to justify why it costs what it costs.

Confidence matters. So does how you present the investment.

State your price clearly. Explain the payment options. Give your prospect space to make a decision without nervously filling every second with more words.

And remember: silence is not your enemy.

You don't need to convince someone by talking faster or harder. You need to communicate the value clearly, answer their questions honestly, and let them decide whether it's the right fit.

Own your price. Present it with confidence. Then stop talking and listen.

They say you don’t know true heartbreak until it becomes physical. 

I’ve experienced loss before, but nothing prepared me for the weight of this week.

On New Year’s Eve, we got the call that my dad wouldn’t make it through the night. 

My brother, sister, and I dropped everything and drove seven hours to Savannah. We pulled into the hospital parking lot at exactly 12:01 AM.

Fireworks were exploding over the city to celebrate a New Year, while we were walking in to say goodbye to the man who gave us life. 

It was the most surreal moment of my existence.

Transparently, our relationship wasn’t always easy. 

We were both built with the same unrelenting standards.

Two people with a specific vision of how things should be, often to a fault. 

Sometimes the very conviction that made us both successful was the thing that kept us at a distance.

But as I look at the life I’ve built: the drive, the resilience, the refusal to settle for anything but the best, I see his fingerprints everywhere.

My dad came to this country at 18 with less than $20 in his pocket. 

He built a life that was captured in magazines and defined by a level of excellence I strive for every day. 

When he first fought cancer 9 years ago, I was his primary caretaker. 

We were best friends then, and those remain the fondest memories of my life. 

It was seeing his fragility then that gave me the courage to choose freedom over a “safe” path.

I owe the life I love today to him.

My grandma passed during Diwali, the Indian New Year. 

It feels only fitting that Dad chose New Year’s Day to join her.

To my brother and sister, Nikhil and Ahna: I am so grateful for your strength. 

We’ve been each other’s anchors, and I couldn’t have navigated this surreal walk without you.

Rest easy, Dad. I see you in the parts of me I love the most. 

To the moon and back.
